catalog_quote: 3. Tones 1. Lexical tones Like most Bantu languages of the zone, Mokpe contrasts two lexical basic tones: the low and the high ( ´). However, a downstepped high tone ( ꜝ́), the falling ( ˆ) and the rising ( ˇ) are equally noted. The falling and the rising are the results of the combination of the two basic tones. Example: Low: ŋmà "year", wɔ̀kpɔ̀ "beard", lìkpàmbà "cassava"; High: kɔ́ "snail", ɲáŋgá "sand", ímbúndá "friends"; Falling: lìβê "breast (female)", ɲô "body"; Rising: tǔ "room", lìmě "to swallow", mɔ̌lèŋgù "sheep" 2. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mokpwe is described as a two-tone (L, H) Bantu language with derived contour tones and downstep, lexical and grammatical tone functions, CV/V syllables; the sketch gives no role to word stress or accent and never mentions either. Corroborated by Monikang 1989 (ch. 5, pp. 66-80: prosody = vowel length + tone; p. 92 'Mokpwe is a language with four tones (high, low, rising, and falling)') and Kagaya 1992 (sec. 2-3: L and H contrastive underlyingly), none of which states a stress position or explicitly denies stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes only: downstepped H; word-final L after L realized super-low/falling at the intonational level (Kagaya 1992); Meeussen's Rule lowering the second of two H (Atindogbe 2013 pp. 20-21).
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern lexical/grammatical tone on words in citation form and short phrases; no source distinguishes word-level from phrase-level prominence or discusses stress at any level. Absence of a stress statement is an argument from silence across three independent phonological descriptions (1989, 1992, 2013), not an explicit 'no stress' claim.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the same language (Glottolog mokp1239, ISO bri; names Mokpwe/Mokpe/Mòkpè/Bakweri/Bakwiri/Bakueri/Kpe, Guthrie A22). Atindogbe 2013 is based on Buea-area speech; Kagaya's informants are from Voba and Bonakanda villages near Buea; Monikang 1989 is a University of Yaounde diploma dissertation on 'Mokpwe' (MPG record also tags bwt Bafaw-Balong, but the thesis itself is on Mokpwe/Bakweri only). No dialect-level glottocodes involved.

sources.note: Phonology chapter (pp. 8-23: sounds, tones, syllable structure, phonological rules, tonal rules, orthography) treats prosody purely as tone: p.11 'Mokpe contrasts two lexical basic tones: the low and the high' plus downstepped H, falling, rising; grammatical tones; tone rules (deletion, copy, simplification, Meeussen). The words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the 163 pages; no statement on word stress.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 66-80) opens with a generic definition listing 'stress, tone and duration' as prosodic features, then limits itself to vowel length (5.1, marginal) and tone (5.2-5.4: two register tones L/H, rising and falling combinations, downdrift, grammatical tone). Conclusion p.92: 'Mokpwe is a language with four tones (high, low, rising, and falling)'. No statement about where stress falls or whether it exists.
